title: Context read (ZIFFER-SPEC-001 section 8.7, section 8.8; raise-only per section 8.3.2 TR-2/TR-3)
description:
One snapshot-consistent read of the Context Store, carried on legs F3.1 (Context Store -> Policy Engine) and F3.5 (Context Store -> Executor) of the flow-leg register (ZIFFER-DEPLOY-001 Annex A). Section 8.7 requires that Context reads be snapshot-consistent, which is why ONE read is ONE object carrying every fact read under ONE `snapshot_hash`, rather than a separate response per function of the section 8.8 interface. Split into per-function responses, a Policy Engine can answer capability at evaluation-order step 4 from one snapshot and tier at step 7 from another, and the consistency section 8.7 requires holds of neither.

THE RULE THIS OBJECT EXISTS TO CARRY, AND THE ONE A CONSUMER MUST NOT GET WRONG: A CONTEXT READ RAISES, AND CAN NEVER LOWER. TR-1 puts a resource's floor tier in the signed bundle (`floors.json`), read-only to the runtime under PB-4. TR-2 lets the Context Store serve a RAISE and nothing else. TR-3 composes them at the consumer: `effective_tier(r) = max(floor(r), raise(r))`, absent raise = T0, and evaluation order step 7 states the same composition. Because risk functions only escalate (RK-3), TR-4 is then a theorem rather than a hope: a compromised Context Store can drive effective tier UP, producing more attestation, which is safe, and can never drive it below the signed floor. It is mechanized as `FloorDominance` (Annex B, theorem 2, SMT-discharged over the 4x4 lattice and killed by mutation M1), and section 4.3 classes the Context Store on exactly that basis -- 'Trusted for RAISES only. Cannot lower effective tier.'

WHAT BREAKS IF A CONSUMER TREATS THIS OBJECT AS ABLE TO LOWER. The whole of v1.2.0's most serious defect returns, and section 8.3.2 opens by naming it: tier data in two mutually exclusive places, so RK-5's two-person control over floor changes protects a copy that does not feed evaluation. That is C2, and its attack is T-16, tier suppression -- falsify a resource's tier downward and the escalation trigger never fires, so a floor-T3 action grades LOW, takes step 11's ALLOW branch, and executes with no quorum. INV-1-HIGH is stated over floor-only risk (TR-5) precisely so that no single runtime component can forge it downward; a consumer that took an effective tier, or a floor, from this object would move the value back under the control of the component section 10's invariant table says must not have it. Annex B's proof would still discharge, and it would be a proof about a composition the implementation no longer performs. Note also which direction is cheap: TR-9 makes lowering a floor an offline-key deploy under RK-5 while raising stays fast through this object, and that asymmetry is the design.

WHAT IS NOT A FIELD, EACH ABSENT ON PURPOSE. (1) A FLOOR TIER, and (2) AN EFFECTIVE TIER. The floor is TR-1's, comes from the signed bundle the consumer already holds, and a second copy of it here is C2 restated at the wire; the effective tier is TR-3's `max`, which the consumer computes, and a transmitted one is a derived security value accepted from the party under verification (TR-8's rule, RES-8's wording). (3) A `granted: false` capability answer -- see `capability_grants`. (4) THE PROVIDER CLASS. CP-1 declares provider selection per tenant IN THE SIGNED BUNDLE, and CP-3 requires evaluation logic to be identical across providers; a provider class carried here is both a value read from the party being verified and a field a consumer could branch on, and CP-3 forbids the branch. (5) A TENANT IDENTIFIER. DP-43 puts tenant separation for the Context Store at the CREDENTIAL boundary -- a credential scoped to one tenant must not be able to read another tenant's rows -- so tenancy is a property of the connection rather than a claim in the payload. A claimed `tenant_id` would be self-asserted scope from the store, which is the same shape again. The residual is real and is disclosed rather than closed: nothing in the payload lets a consumer detect a store that answered with another tenant's facts, and DP-78 already records that this repository reads no credential domain and can audit no such boundary. (6) A SIGNATURE. WE-1 makes COSE_Sign1 the receipt's carrier and AT-8a pins the Attestation Object's encoding; no clause states a signature over a Context read. Section 4.3 authenticates this leg at the transport (mTLS REQUIRED between components) and accepts the store as trusted-for-raises-only, which is coherent only because a compromised store fails safe in both available directions. Section 8.7.1's 'Context Store signing key SHOULD be in an offline HSM' is INFORMATIVE and names no bytes it signs, so a `signature` property here would invent an envelope the specification does not have.

WHY THE FIELD SET IS CLOSED, AND WHY THAT CLAIM IS WEAKER HERE THAN IT IS FOR THE ATTESTATION OBJECT. `additionalProperties` is false and every property is required. NO CLAUSE STATES THIS RULE. AT-8b closes the Attestation Object's field set and calls the closure the security property itself; there is no AT-8b for a Context read. Closure is adopted because it is the fail-safe direction -- an unknown key is refused rather than ignored, a missing key is refused rather than defaulted -- and because of Z4: any optional field gives one read two valid encodings, and the receipt carries `context_snapshot_hash` (AT-1, section 9.2) as a name for exactly this object, so two encodings of one snapshot are two names for it. That argument is CONDITIONAL on a preimage the specification does not define (see `snapshot_hash`), which is why it is recorded as a gap rather than presented as a reading. The consequence of an optional field here is therefore not Z4's amplification but DIVERGENCE: one consumer refuses the unknown key, another ignores it, and at a verifier a divergence is indistinguishable from a compromise.

ENCODING IS NOT PINNED BY ANY CLAUSE, AND THAT IS A HOLE RATHER THAN A CHOICE. Section 9.2 pins JCS (RFC 8785) for the Proposal and canonical CBOR (RFC 8949 section 4.2) for the receipt and the Attestation Object (WE-1, WE-2, AT-8a). Nothing pins a canonicalization for the Context read, and section 8.8 gives `snapshot_hash()` a return type and never a preimage. So the one artifact in this register whose digest is carried inside a signed receipt is the one artifact with no stated canonical form. The JSON below is written as diagnostic form, in the same sense WE-3 gives that phrase for receipts, and it is NOT an assertion that JSON is the wire form; no clause says what the wire form is.

SUITE 12 CLASSIFICATION. Every field below is class T at the schema layer, because this document constrains SHAPE and shape is not authority. Two of them are T at the SYSTEM layer as well, with residuals the specification already discloses rather than residuals this file is introducing. Capability facts: section 8.7's note and section 10's invariant table state that a compromised Context Store can withhold a capability (DENY, safe), raise a tier (more attestation, safe), or FALSIFY A GRANT AT MEDIUM, which is INV-1-MEDIUM's disclosed residual -- INV-1-HIGH survives because floor-HIGH already required a quorum and step 9 is a revocation recheck closing the issuance-to-execution window (T-10), not the authorization itself. `snapshot_hash`: TR-10's rule is that a transmitted identifier is a NAME for a binding and not EVIDENCE of one, and this identifier is not merely unverified but unverifiable, because no clause says what it covers.

WHAT THIS SCHEMA DOES NOT CONSTRAIN, listed so that shape validity is never read as conformance. (a) SNAPSHOT CONSISTENCY (section 8.7) is a property of how the facts were read, not of the object; a store that assembles a `ContextRead` from three different snapshots and stamps one hash on it is shape-valid here. (b) THE FRESHNESS BOUND. CP-2 resolves stale freshness to DENY and L-18 caps revocation staleness at 5 minutes, but the contract that applies is the one section 8.8's provider table gives for the bundle-declared provider class (CP-1), so the bound is evaluated by the consumer against the signed bundle and never parsed here -- see `freshness_seconds`. (c) THAT THE READ IS LIVE. Step 9 requires the Executor to RE-QUERY at execution time; a cached `ContextRead` replayed inside its freshness window is indistinguishable from a fresh one at this layer, and that is the whole of T-10. (d) THAT THE ANSWERS MATCH THE QUESTIONS. The specification defines no query message, so nothing binds this response to the read that was requested. (e) ORDERING, of `capability_grants` or of anything else.

NOTHING IN THIS REPOSITORY PRODUCES OR CONSUMES THIS OBJECT, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT. The Python reference models Context as an in-process dict of operator -> set of `"task_type:target"` strings (`acp_executor.py`, `Executor.context`), read once at step 9. It implements none of section 8.8's four functions: there is no `snapshot_hash()`, no `freshness()`, and `tier_raise` appears nowhere in `reference/` or `crates/` -- both evaluators bind `resource.effective_tier` to the FLOOR (TR-5's floor-only computation), so TR-3's `max` has no implementation anywhere and the raise half of the floor/raise model is proof and prose only. `context_snapshot_hash` appears in every fixture as the literal string `"sha256:ctx"`, which does not even match the `sha256` type this file references. ACP-52 already records that nothing validates a fixture against these schemas; DP-57 records that the fail-closed response to an unreachable or stale Context Store is a normative MUST with NOTHING in this repository that goes red when it is violated. Per DP-86 a component gets a register row whether or not anyone built it, and by the same argument it gets a schema.

snapshot_hash.description:
The identifier of the snapshot every fact in this object was read from (section 8.8, `snapshot_hash() -> sha256`). It is what the Decision carries forward as `context_snapshot_hash` in the receipt (section 9.2) and inside every Attestation Object (AT-1), so the value a human attester's device shows and signs over is this one.

IT IS A NAME FOR A BINDING, NOT EVIDENCE OF ONE (TR-10; RES-8 is the dossier's wording of the same rule). Worse than the usual case: it is not merely unverified, it is UNVERIFIABLE. Section 8.8 declares the return type and no clause anywhere says WHAT BYTES the digest covers or under which canonicalization, so no consumer can recompute it, no two implementations can be shown to agree on it, and a store is free to emit a constant. The consequence is that the receipt's `context_snapshot_hash` -- a field carried through the signed body and through the attested object, the field that is supposed to say WHICH Context the Decision was computed over -- discharges nothing today. Section 9.3's checklist has no step that reads it, which is consistent: there is nothing to check it against.

This is a normative gap found by writing the schema rather than by reading the text, which is the same way AT-1's `b64:` nonce type was found to be unstated (ACP-87, closed at the root as WE-4 in v1.3.18). It is recorded here and NOT closed here: pinning a preimage in a schema would make this file the definition of a type the specification does not have, and a second implementation written from the document alone would never see it.

freshness_seconds.description:
The age of the last authoritative update behind this read, in whole seconds (section 8.8, `freshness() -> age of last authoritative update`). CP-2 makes it a control input rather than telemetry: all providers MUST honour P-4, and stale freshness resolves to DENY with a distinct reason code -- unknown is never LOW. What the bound IS depends on the provider class the signed bundle declares for the tenant (CP-1) and on section 8.8's provider table: a static signed entitlement bundle has staleness near zero, workload attestation is per-request, and live directory sync must be within L-18's 5 minutes for revocations or the sync is broken and the deployment fails closed.

THERE IS NO MAXIMUM HERE, DELIBERATELY. Encoding L-18 as a schema bound would turn a control decision into a parse error: the consumer must DENY with P-4's distinct reason code, and a malformed-message rejection loses the reason code, loses the audit record of a Decision that was refused for staleness, and applies the live-sync bound to providers section 8.8 gives a different contract. `minimum` is 0 because an age cannot be negative and a value outside the domain MUST refuse rather than take the permissive branch -- EL-2 states that reading for the evaluation environment and P-4 states it generally; a negative age read as 'very fresh' is the permissive branch arriving through a type error.

THE NAME AND THE UNIT ARE THIS FILE'S, NOT THE SPECIFICATION'S, AND BOTH ARE GAPS. Section 8.8 names the function `freshness()` and its return 'age of last authoritative update'; it fixes no unit, no wire type and no name, so `_seconds` is carried in the field name because a bare duration with its unit in a comment is a unit nobody reads.

AND THE RES-8 OBJECTION, STATED RATHER THAN SILENTLY FIXED. An AGE is computed by the Context Store, on the Context Store's clock, and the staleness decision that fires CP-2's DENY is then keyed on a derived value supplied by the party being read -- TR-8's shape exactly. Carrying the INSTANT of the last authoritative update instead would let the consumer derive the age against its own NTS-disciplined clock within the L-20 skew allowance, which is what section 12.5 and leg F9.1 exist to make available, and would move this row from 'derived value accepted as transmitted' to 'raw fact plus consumer-computed derivation'. This file models the return type section 8.8 states. Changing it is a text change, and making it silently inside a schema is how a register acquires a claim nobody decided (the ACP-86 shape).

capability_grants.description:
The capability facts this snapshot asserts: one entry per (operator, capability, resource) triple that `has_capability` answered TRUE for (section 8.8). Consumed at evaluation-order step 4 (operator holds every required capability, else DENY) and again at section 9.3 step 9, where for recomputed floor-HIGH the Executor re-queries capability of the operator established in step 7b(iii-a) -- taken from the verified Attestation Object, never from the receipt body -- and fails closed if it has been revoked.

THERE IS NO BOOLEAN, AND ABSENCE IS THE ANSWER. `has_capability` returns a bool, but under P-4 and CP-2 the two false-ish outcomes are ONE outcome: an unknown operator, an unknown resource and a capability the store simply declined to assert all resolve to DENY. Representing them differently would give one outcome two encodings while no decision anywhere depends on the difference -- two spellings of one thing, which is the defect class this repository is built around, and here it would also split the snapshot digest.

`uniqueItems` because a repeated grant is a second spelling of one fact. Note that a grant's identity is the WHOLE TRIPLE, which is why `x-acp-keyed-by` is deliberately absent: a lookup keyed by `operator` alone answers 'granted' for the wrong capability on the wrong resource, and a generator that emitted one would be building the vulnerability. That used to cost a check that would not run: `tools/codegen.py` read an array's `x-acp-absent` only alongside `x-acp-keyed-by`, so the fail-safe declared below was dropped in silence -- a rule written down that reached nothing, with every gate green. It was declared anyway, because the schema is the normative artifact and the rule belongs in it, and the gap was disclosed rather than worked around by mis-keying the lookup. ACP-78 M1 closed it from the generator's side: an array carrying an absent rule with no key now HALTS in the root that emits accessors, and in this root the rule is carried into the generated field's documentation. No multi-field key was invented, because the key is the decision and inventing it here would be building the vulnerability.

No `maxItems`. L-05 bounds list length at ingress, on a request; a Context read is not a request, and a store whose honest answer exceeds an invented cap would have to truncate, which silently converts grants into DENYs.

x-acp-absent.why: a triple absent from this list is a capability the snapshot does not assert, and P-4's default is DENY: no matching rule, unknown capability, unclassified resource and unavailable Context Store each refuse, with a distinct reason code. CP-2 binds every provider class to that rule. An accessor that returns a bare Option here is one unwrap away from treating 'the store said nothing' as 'the store said yes', which at section 9.3 step 9 is a revoked operator executing a floor-HIGH action. NO ACCESSOR IS GENERATED FOR THIS LIST AND THE RULE IS CARRIED AS DOCUMENTATION (the wire root's `absent_emits` is `doc`), so the sentence above describes what a CONSUMER must do rather than what a generated lookup does for it. Two things forced that. A grant's identity is the whole triple `(operator, capability, resource)` -- section 8.8's `has_capability` takes all three -- and `x-acp-keyed-by` names ONE field, so a generated lookup keyed by any single one of them answers 'granted' for the wrong resource, which is building the vulnerability rather than typing it. And ACP-78 M1 found that an array's `x-acp-absent` was read only ALONGSIDE `x-acp-keyed-by`: declared without a key it was dropped in silence, which is the failure the generator's keyword audit refuses one level up. That is now a HALT in the root that emits accessors.

tier_raises.description:
Resource identifier -> RAISE tier (section 8.8, `tier_raise(resource) -> T0..T3`; TR-2). A RAISE and nothing else: the consumer holds the floor from the signed bundle (TR-1) and computes `effective_tier(r) = max(floor(r), raise(r))` itself (TR-3, evaluation order step 7). Absent raise is T0, so an unclassified resource is governed entirely by its floor -- which under RK-1 is T3 when `floors.json` does not name it. The two defaults compose in the safe direction on purpose: absent floor is the HIGHEST tier, absent raise is the LOWEST, because the floor is the value a compromised runtime must not be able to lower and the raise is the value it must not be able to invent downward.

The key space is `floors.json`'s key space and the bound is copied from `floors.schema.json` for that reason: TR-3's `max` is taken over the two maps keyed by the same resource identifier, so a resource nameable in one map and unnameable in the other has no defined effective tier. It is an open map for the same reason floors is -- resources are deployment-specific -- and the VALUES are closed.

A T0 ENTRY AND AN ABSENT ENTRY MEAN THE SAME THING, AND THE SPECIFICATION PERMITS BOTH. TR-2 gives the return type as T0..T3 and TR-3 makes `max(floor, T0) = floor`, so an explicit T0 is a second encoding of 'no raise'. The enum is not narrowed to T1..T3 here because narrowing the stated range would be this file exceeding the document; the consequence is recorded instead, and it is Z4-shaped -- two encodings of one snapshot are two `snapshot_hash` values for it, in whatever preimage a future clause defines.

x-acp-absent.why: TR-3 states it in as many words: absent raise = T0. This is the one place in this file where the LOWEST value is the fail-safe one, and the reason is that the raise is not the tier -- the floor is, it comes from the signed bundle, and RK-1 already defaults an unnamed resource to T3. A lookup that refused here, or that defaulted upward, would let a silent Context Store escalate every resource it has never heard of and hand a compromised store a denial of service against the attestation queue that AQ-1 to AQ-3 exist to protect. THIS OBJECT SETTLED A TENSION INSIDE THE GENERATOR AND THE ANSWER IS WORTH READING WITH THE RULE. `tools/codegen.py` HALTED on a map with no absent rule -- every table a caller can miss needs its absent case stated in the schema -- while its wire-root header note said no fail-safe accessor should be emitted in that root at all, because an absent rule on a wire field would be a default supplied by the party under verification. This is the only MESSAGE in the register that is a LOOKUP TABLE, so it is the case neither was written for. ACP-78 M1 resolved it per root: the wire root declares `absent_emits="doc"`, the rule below is CARRIED into the generated field's documentation, and NO accessor is emitted. The deciding argument is one root over: `floors.schema.json` already generates the accessor that answers T3 on a miss (RK-1, P-4), and a second generated accessor answering T0 on a miss over a TRANSMITTED map would put the permissive answer behind an API shaped like a control, one import away from the signed one. The rule stated here is TR-3's and is right; where it has effect is in the consumer's `max(floor, raise)`, against a floor that came from the signed bundle.

capability_grant.description: One asserted answer of `has_capability(operator, capability, resource)` (section 8.8). All three arguments are carried because all three identify the fact: an entry naming fewer of them answers a question nobody asked, and at section 9.3 step 9 the question is specific -- capability of THIS operator on THIS target. The reference implementation is the counterexample and it is worth keeping in view: `acp_executor.py` keys capabilities by the joined string `f"{task_type}:{target}"`, so a capability name containing a colon aliases a different (capability, resource) pair, and the three-argument interface section 8.8 declares has no three-argument representation anywhere in the reference.

operator.description: The principal the capability is asserted for. This is the SAME value the Attestation Object carries as `operator` and the same one section 9.3 step 7b(iii-a) hands to step 9, so the bound is copied from `attestation_object.schema.json` rather than chosen: if the two disagreed, an operator an attestation can name would be an operator this read cannot answer for, and step 9 could not run. Neither bound is stated by the specification -- see the note on `resource`.

capability.description: The capability asserted. Section 8.8 names this argument and nothing anywhere declares its identifier space, its syntax or its relation to a rule's required capabilities at evaluation-order step 4; the bound is the neighbouring one rather than a fourth invention.

resource.description: The resource the capability is asserted over -- the same identifier space `floors.json` and `tier_raises` are keyed by, so the bound is copied from `floors.schema.json`. THE SPECIFICATION BOUNDS NO IDENTIFIER LENGTH ANYWHERE except L-04's 2,048-character maximum string field, whose enforcement point is 'Schema' and whose scope (a Proposal's fields, or every string on every wire) it does not state. Three schemas in this repository already pin three different bounds. Copying a neighbour's is the least bad of the available moves and is not a reading of the document.
